structure.rationale: The ten user-supplied chapters (kept in the requester's order) move from the frame to the machinery to the system: first the architectural principles every later trade-off is judged against (layering, end-to-end, fate sharing, control/data/management planes, per Saltzer-Reed-Clark and Clark '88); then the data plane inside one box (forwarding), then how many boxes agree on paths (routing), then how endpoints share those paths (transport) and how the network arbitrates contention (queues, AQM, scheduling, QoS). Security follows once the reader knows every mechanism an attacker can abuse. SDN, virtualization/cloud and wireless/edge are three re-arrangements of the same planes under new constraints (central control, multi-tenancy, scarce and moving capacity). Measurement and operations close the loop and host the capstone case studies, which reuse every earlier chapter.
structure.audience: Expert readers who already understand fundamental networking (packets, IP addressing, the layer model, basic TCP); they want architectural trade-offs, protocol internals, quantitative reasoning, security, virtualization and operational practice — delivered in the thing-explainer plain-words voice without losing technical precision.

claims.text: Layering gives each layer a service interface to the one above and hides how the layer below works, so implementations can change independently; the Internet's stack is often drawn as an hourglass with IP as the narrow waist.

Akhshabi & Dovrolis's EvoArch model reproduces the hourglass shape from almost any starting stack; the surviving waist protocols (IPv4; TCP and UDP) are old and widely depended on, not necessarily the highest-quality ones.

RFC 1958 (Carpenter, 1996) summarizes the community view: the goal is connectivity, the tool is the Internet Protocol, and the intelligence is end to end rather than hidden in the network; it notes the Internet grew by evolution, not from a grand plan.

The end-to-end argument (Saltzer, Reed, Clark 1984): a function that can be completely and correctly implemented only with knowledge at the endpoints cannot be provided correctly by the communication system alone; low-level versions are justified only as performance enhancements.

The paper's careful-file-transfer example: threats include disk faults, buffering/copy bugs in host software, and host crashes, which per-hop network reliability cannot catch; the robust fix is an end-to-end checksum check and retry. Making each step triple-redundant is judged uneconomical.

Clark (1988) lists the DARPA Internet's goals in priority order: survivability despite loss of networks/gateways; multiple types of service; variety of networks; distributed management; cost effectiveness; low-effort host attachment; accountability. The ordering came from the military context, and the later goals were met least well.
Fate-sharing (Clark 1988): keep connection state at the endpoints, so state is lost only if the entity that cares about it is also lost; gateways can then be stateless datagram switches.

Clark (1988) records that TCP and IP were originally one protocol and were split so that services not wanting reliable byte streams (e.g. packet voice, debugging) could run over IP via UDP — the 'multiple types of service' goal.

In October 1986 the Internet suffered the first of a series of congestion collapses: throughput between LBL and UC Berkeley (sites about 400 yards apart) fell from 32 kb/s to 40 b/s. The fix (slow start, congestion avoidance, better RTT estimation) was placed in end hosts' TCP, not in routers.

RFC 3439 (Bush & Meyer, 2002) names complexity the main barrier to scaling and states a Simplicity Principle, an Amplification Principle (large systems show non-linearities small ones don't; small things can cause huge events) and a Coupling Principle; its section 3 is 'Layering Considered Harmful', warning that stacking layers adds optimization and feature-richness costs.

Cross-layer designs can create unplanned feedback loops and interaction effects that threaten stability, and unstructured cross-layer coupling produces 'spaghetti' architectures that are hard to maintain and that block later innovation.

RFC 7426 separates the forwarding (data) plane, which handles packets per their rules, from the control plane, which decides those rules for one or more devices, and from the management plane, which monitors, configures and maintains devices; it also names an operational plane for a device's overall operating state, and contrasts control vs management by timescale.

Middleboxes constrain protocol evolution: Honda et al. measured paths that rewrite initial sequence numbers, strip or pass unknown TCP options and resegment data, so new TCP extensions (e.g. MPTCP) must be designed to survive them — 'ossification'.
Encrypting transport headers (as QUIC does) helps avoid ossification by middleboxes and hides transport behaviour from the path, at the cost of operator visibility.

RFC 9413 (IAB, 2023) argues that tolerating unexpected input under the robustness principle ('be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept') causes long-term interoperability harm, and recommends active protocol maintenance instead.

Tussle in Cyberspace: stakeholders (users, ISPs, governments, rights holders) have conflicting interests; the architecture should 'design for variation in outcome' — modularize along tussle boundaries and design for choice — rather than dictate one outcome, because rigid designs get broken.

Per-frame overhead for TCP over Ethernet with a 1500-byte MTU: 8 B preamble/SFD + 14 B header + 4 B FCS + 12 B inter-frame gap = 38 B on the wire; IPv4 20 B + TCP 20 B + timestamps 12 B leave 1448 B of payload, so goodput is 1448/1538 ≈ 94.1% of line rate; a 100-byte application message is ≈ 52.6%.

Retry cost arithmetic: with n hops each losing a packet with probability p, end-to-end-only retry succeeds per attempt with probability (1-p)^n and costs on average ((1-(1-p)^n)/p)/(1-p)^n link transmissions, versus n/(1-p) with per-hop retry. n=10,p=1%: 10.6 vs 10.1; n=10,p=10%: 18.7 vs 11.1; n=5,p=30%: 16.5 vs 7.1. This is why lossy links (e.g. Wi-Fi) add link-layer retransmission as a performance enhancement while TCP keeps the end-to-end check.

Availability arithmetic: five components in series at 99.9% each give ≈ 99.50%; two such paths in parallel give ≈ 99.9975% only if their failures are independent — shared fate (same conduit, same software bug, same config push) erases the gain.
Data-plane time budget at 400 Gb/s: a full 1538-byte on-wire frame lasts ≈30.8 ns and a minimum 84-byte on-wire frame ≈1.7 ns, so per-packet work must be fixed-function or pipelined.
Routers police the traffic punted from the data plane to the control-plane CPU (control-plane protection / policing), because flooding that path starves routing protocols.
QUIC connection IDs let a connection survive address changes and let load balancers route without per-connection memory of the 5-tuple.

pitfalls: Reading the end-to-end argument as 'never put function in the network' — the paper explicitly allows in-network versions as performance enhancements; it says they cannot replace the endpoint check.

Treating the OSI 7-layer model as the Internet's architecture; the Internet's working shape is the hourglass around IP, and real systems routinely violate strict layering (NAT, PMTUD, TCP checksum over an IP pseudo-header).
Assuming redundant paths are independent; shared conduits, software and config pushes create correlated failures.
Equating SDN's control/data separation with 'centralization' — the separation is about interfaces; a separated control plane can still be distributed.
Assuming cross-layer optimization is free: it couples layers, creates feedback loops, and freezes the interface it peeks through.

claims.text: A forwarding element's per-packet pipeline is: parse headers, classify/look up (exact, longest-prefix, ternary matches), modify (rewrite MAC, decrement TTL, push/pop labels), then queue and schedule onto the output port; the control plane only fills the tables.
Minimum-size Ethernet frame is 64 B plus 8 B preamble/SFD and 12 B inter-frame gap = 84 B (672 bits) on the wire; at 100 Gb/s that is ~148.8 M packets/s, ~6.7 ns per packet; at 400 Gb/s ~1.68 ns.

Longest-prefix match: an IP destination may match several prefixes; the most specific (longest) wins. The global IPv4 BGP table passed one million prefixes in 2025 (APNIC counted 1,001,332 on 8 May 2025), and the count varies by vantage point.

DIR-24-8 (Gupta, Lin, McKeown 1998): a 2^24-entry first table indexed by the top 24 address bits, plus a second table for longer prefixes; most lookups take one memory access, the rest two; the first table is ~32 MB. DPDK's LPM library uses a variant.

A TCAM stores value+mask per entry and compares the key against every entry in parallel in one cycle; a priority encoder returns the first match, so storing prefixes ordered by length gives longest-prefix match in one access, but inserts may have to move entries to keep the order.

TCAM costs several times more area per bit than SRAM and burns far more power because every search charges every match line; one model gives ~3 µW per bit, and an 18 Mb TCAM at 100–150 MHz is quoted at 10 W or more versus 1–2 W for SRAM.

Exact-match tables (MAC, five-tuple flow tables) are built from hashing into SRAM; ECMP picks among equal-cost next hops by hashing flow fields (hash-threshold in RFC 2992), keeping a flow on one path to avoid reordering at the cost of uneven load when flows differ in size.

With one FIFO per input, head-of-line blocking limits throughput of an N×N input-queued switch under uniform saturated traffic to 2 − √2 ≈ 58.6% as N grows large (Karol, Hluchyj, Morgan 1987); for small N it is higher (0.75 at N=2, ~0.655 at N=4, ~0.618 at N=8).

Virtual output queues (one queue per output at each input) remove HOL blocking; iSLIP, an iterative round-robin matching scheduler, reaches 100% throughput for uniform traffic and never starves a queue; schedulers were built for 32 ports at ~100 M decisions/s.
Pure output queueing needs the output memory to accept up to N packets per slot (N× speedup), which is why high-port-count switches use input/VOQ or shared-memory designs with modest fabric speedup.

Store-and-forward receives the whole frame and checks the FCS before sending, adding one serialization delay per hop (1500 B at 10 Gb/s = 1.2 µs); cut-through starts sending after the header, so latency is roughly independent of frame length, but corrupt frames propagate and cut-through is impossible when the egress is faster than the ingress or the egress is busy.

The buffer rule of thumb is RTT × C; Appenzeller et al. showed a link carrying n long-lived desynchronized TCP flows needs about RTT × C / √n, e.g. a 2.5 Gb/s link with 10,000 flows could cut buffers ~99%; the 2019 Redux paper notes the result changed practice only partly.

RMT (Bosshart et al. 2013): a programmable parser plus 32 physical match-action stages on a 1 GHz pipeline handling 960 M packets/s for 64×10 Gb ports; tables in each stage are built from SRAM (exact match) and TCAM (ternary) blocks; the authors estimate programmability costs ~15% chip area and ~12% power over a fixed-function chip.

P4_16 programs declare headers, a parser state machine, match-action tables with actions, and control blocks that apply tables; the architecture (e.g. v1model, PSA, TNA) fixes what blocks a target exposes. The current spec is v1.2.5 (2024).

Intel announced in January 2023 it would stop developing new Tofino switch ASICs while continuing to sell and support Tofino and Tofino 2; P4 remains used on SmartNICs/DPUs, FPGAs and software targets.
Fixed-function merchant switch ASICs keep doubling: Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 (shipping from June 2025) is a single-chip 102.4 Tb/s switch with up to 512×200G or 1024×100G ports.

SmartNICs/DPUs put programmable packet engines plus general-purpose cores (e.g. NVIDIA BlueField-3: Arm cores, up to 400 Gb/s) on the NIC, so the host's infrastructure work — virtual switching, encryption, storage — runs off the host CPU; AMD Pensando and Intel IPUs are similar parts.

Line-rate hardware is a fixed budget per packet: each pipeline stage gets a fixed number of clock cycles and a fixed number of memory accesses, so programs that need loops, unbounded state or many dependent lookups do not fit; this is why P4 has no loops in the control flow and parsers are bounded state machines.

On 12 August 2014 ('512K day') the IPv4 table briefly passed 512,000 routes after a burst of ~15,000 deaggregated routes; older routers whose default hardware (TCAM) partition held ~512K IPv4 routes overflowed, causing scattered outages, though the vendor had warned beforehand and the fix was a reconfiguration plus reboot.

Packets a hardware parser cannot handle at line rate (e.g. IPv4 options, unusually deep header stacks) are typically punted to a slower CPU path or dropped, which discourages new header formats in the middle of the network.
Broadcom also ships a co-packaged-optics Tomahawk 6 variant (Davisson), moving optical I/O next to the switch die to cut I/O power.
Derived figure: a 102.4 Tb/s chip at 672 bits per minimum-size packet would face ≈1.52×10^11 packets/s if every port ran smallest packets.

snippets.note: P4_16, v1model architecture (as in the p4lang tutorials); forward/drop actions defined elsewhere

pitfalls: Line rate is usually quoted for large packets; small-packet (64 B) rates are the hard case and many boxes cannot do them on every port at once.
The FIB (in the data plane) is not the RIB (in the control plane); a router can hold more routes in software than its hardware tables fit, and overflow means slow-path or dropped traffic.
58.6% is the large-N, uniform, saturated, fixed-cell limit; real HOL loss depends on traffic.
Cut-through only helps when the output is idle and no faster than the input; under load every switch is store-and-forward.
RTT×C/√n assumes many desynchronized long flows; it does not apply to data-center incast or links with few flows.
ECMP hashing keeps flows in order but a few elephant flows can collide on one link; same hash function on every tier causes polarization.
